source: Agreed with the repo owner, 2026-09-04. The Dungeons & Dividends rulebook (§13 item 3) explicitly leaves sub-stat scoring unspecified: 'Exact sub-stat scoring formulas (real dollars/inputs -> 8-20 scores) — this is the one piece the Claude Code build prompt still needs.' These are that missing piece.
confidenceNote: Calibration target: a US-population-median household scores 10 on every computed sub-stat, per the rulebook's own reading of 10-11 as 'neutral / average'. Median anchors are set from widely-published public figures (Census/BLS median earnings, BEA personal saving rate, SCF transaction-account balances) but are ROUNDED CONVENTIONS, not fitted distributions. Every other rung is an agreed shape, not a measurement. Edit this file to recalibrate; the engine reads it and holds no thresholds of its own.
note: Ladders interpolate linearly between rungs and clamp to 8-20. A sub-stat whose input was never entered is INCOMPLETE, never 8 and never 0 — see CLAUDE.md 'Empty != zero'.

methods.name: Feats of Strength
methods.blurb: Earn each score. Knowledge questions have right answers; judgment and charisma questions ask for evidence of what you have actually done, not how you rate yourself.

methods.name: Point Buy
methods.blurb: Spend a fixed pool across the nine. Costs escalate at the top exactly as they do in 5e, so a 20 is expensive on purpose.

methods.name: Standard Array
methods.blurb: A fixed spread, assigned where you want it. Fastest honest option when you don't want to answer eighteen questions tonight.

methods.name: Roll
methods.blurb: 4d6, drop the lowest, floored at 8. Rolling cannot reach 19 or 20 — the same ceiling rolling has in 5e.

methods.name: Homebrew
methods.blurb: Type the nine numbers directly. Nothing is checked. For rebuilding a sheet you already trust, or for testing.

pointBuy.note: 8-15 costs are 5e's own table. 16-20 continue the same accelerating curve, since this system allows scores above 15 where 5e point buy does not. A 45-point pool buys all nine at 13, or a sharply peaked spread.

standardArray.note: Nine values averaging 11.3 — deliberately just above the population-median 10, since anyone building a sheet is already more engaged than average.

incomePower.medianAnchor: US median personal earnings for full-time year-round workers, ~$62k. Rounded to $60k = 10.

incomeTrajectory.medianAnchor: Median US nominal wage growth has run near 4%/yr recently and ~3%/yr long-run. 3% = 10, i.e. keeping pace is average.

hustleCapacity.unit: side income as a share of primary income
hustleCapacity.medianAnchor: Roughly a third of US adults report some side income, mostly small. Zero side income with no deployable skill = 8; zero but with a named, ready skill = 10.

readinessBonus.note: Added to the ladder result, then clamped. 'Ready' means a marketable skill named AND a stated willingness to deploy it inside a month.

liquidityAgility.unit: share of total assets reachable in a week without penalty
liquidityAgility.medianAnchor: Median US household holds very little outside home equity and retirement accounts; a ~10% penalty-free-liquid share is typical. 0.10 = 10.

structuralMobility.medianAnchor: Base 8 plus up to 12 checklist points. A median owner with modest equity, on-site work and a location tie lands near 10.

options.label: I own with less than 20% equity
I owe more than the place is worth

checklist.question: Where your income can be earned from

options.label: Fully remote — location is irrelevant to my pay
Hybrid — I could stretch the radius
Yes, if the case were strong

checklist.question: What ties you to where you live

options.label: Nothing that couldn't move with me
School year, custody, or care obligations
A tie I would not break at any price

obligationFlex.unit: fixed costs as a share of total spending
obligationFlex.medianAnchor: Housing, insurance and required debt service run roughly 60-65% of spending for a typical US household. 0.65 = 10. LOWER is better, so this ladder descends.

savingsRate.medianAnchor: The US personal saving rate has run roughly 4-5% of disposable income. 6% of gross = 10.

consistency.unit: years sustaining the current savings rate
consistency.medianAnchor: One full year at a rate = 10. The rulebook defines this sub-stat as a track record 'through disruption, not just in a good year', so an untested record is capped.
consistency.untestedNote: Without a disruption survived (job loss, medical event, income drop of 20%+) the score is capped at 15 no matter the years, because the rulebook measures this THROUGH disruption.

reserveDepth.medianAnchor: Median US household transaction-account balance covers on the order of 1-1.5 months of spending. 1 month = 10. Rungs above that follow data/liquidity_benchmarks.json bands (3 = the usual floor, 6 = the usual full fund, 12 = deep).

quizNote: Two questions per declared sub-stat, each worth 0-6 points. Score = 8 + the two point values, which lands exactly on the 8-20 scale with no rescaling. An unanswered question leaves the sub-stat INCOMPLETE rather than scoring it low.

hp.note: 1 HP = one week of expenses covered by liquid assets. Agreed with the owner 2026-09-04 to resolve the two incompatible HP definitions in rulebook §3A. See DECISIONS.md D-046.

classAssignment.note: The rulebook names seven levers (§4) but gives no assignment rule. Agreed approach: rank levers by the dollars actually moving through each, break ties on the class's two primary stats. The Keeper is scored on spending restraint rather than a pool, since expense reduction owns no asset.

levers.measure: Employment income (gross annual income less side income)
Spending restraint — how far below a same-income benchmark the household actually spends

classAssignment.keeperNote: The Keeper's 'pool' is the annual dollars NOT spent relative to a benchmark of 75% of gross income going out the door. Someone earning $100k and spending $50k is credited $25k of Keeper activity. This makes an aggressively frugal household able to out-rank a mid-sized portfolio, which is the whole point of the lever.

tier1Affinity.note: NOT rulebook content. The rulebook assigns a class from where money actually moves (§4), which a quiz-only sheet has none of. Ranking on the six main stats does not work either: with only INT, WIS and CHA scored, The Speculator (INT/WIS) is the only class with both primaries available and wins almost every time, while The Landholder (DEX/CON) can never appear at all. So a quiz-only LEANING ranks each class over three of the nine declared sub-stats it has real affinity with. It is explicitly a leaning, shown as such, and is replaced the moment dollars exist.
